# What is causing my oil pan to fill with a mysterious fluid?

When you rebuild an engine, you expect clean oil and predictable behavior. But when the oil level rises again after a fresh change, it's time to look at the chemistry of what's actually in that pan. You've already ruled out coolant because the fluid isn't milky; water mixes with oil to create an emulsion that looks like chocolate milk or mayonnaise. Since your fluid smells like oil, perhaps tinged with gasoline, and doesn't ignite easily, you're likely dealing with fuel contamination.

## How Fuel Gets Into the Oil

In a modern engine with direct injection, fuel is sprayed directly into the cylinder head, so it's physically separated from the crankcase. However, in your 1967 Mustang with a 289 small block V8, you almost certainly have a carburetor or an early throttle-body setup where fuel sits in the intake manifold and cylinders. The path of least resistance for liquid fuel is through the piston rings into the crankcase.

This happens when the engine is running. Fuel vaporizes in the hot cylinder head but doesn't fully burn due to air/fuel mixture issues or incomplete combustion. That unburned fuel washes down the cylinder walls, passes the piston rings, and drops into the oil pan. This is known as "blowby" of liquid fuel, distinct from normal blowby where combustion gases leak past worn rings.

## Why Stagnation Matters More Than You Think

You mentioned the engine sat in the garage for years before your rebuild in 2010, then you rebuilt it recently. Even if the engine was mechanically sound after the rebuild, sitting still changes how fluids behave. Fuel can settle at the bottom of the carburetor bowl or intake manifold and soak into porous materials like rubber gaskets or even the metal walls themselves over time. When you start the engine, that pooled fuel is sucked in immediately.

If the piston rings are stuck closed due to varnish buildup from old fuel, they might not seal properly until the engine warms up. As the engine heats, thermal expansion can momentarily open these rings. However, once the oil pan fills with fuel, you're introducing a new variable: fuel dilution. Gasoline acts as a solvent; it breaks down oil additives and thins the lubricating film. This is why you smell gasoline but don't see immediate failureâthe oil isn't thick enough to protect bearings anymore, even if the engine still runs.

## Confirming Fuel Contamination Without Lab Tests

You tried burning some of the fluid and noted it didn't ignite well. That's a clue. Pure gasoline burns easily; thickened oil with fuel in it doesn't. To confirm this at home without sending samples to a lab, perform a simple density test.

Take a clear container and fill it halfway with your current oil. Then, carefully add an equal amount of fresh oil on top. Seal the container and shake it gently. If the two layers mix immediately and look uniform, you have fuel contamination because gasoline is less dense than oil but mixes completely due to its solvent properties. Coolant would sink or float depending on concentration but wouldn't mix instantly without creating a milky layer.

Alternatively, dip your finger in the oil and run it over white paper. If the stain looks oily but has a distinct lighter ring around the edge, that's fuel evaporating off the surface faster than the heavier oil base.

## Preventing Future Fuel Dilution

The fix isn't just draining the oil; it's addressing why the rings aren't sealing or why so much fuel is unburned. Since you rebuilt the engine in 2010, the rings might have been installed with a light coating of varnish from storage that hardened them shut. Running the engine hard for a few minutes after warming up can help expand the rings and restore their seal.

However, if the carburetor float level is too high or the jets are clogged, you're flooding the cylinders with excess fuel. Check your carburetor settings first. If the issue persists, consider installing an oil separator or using a higher viscosity oil temporarily while you address the root cause.
